Second complete map of a fruit fly brain completed
raw_text: On Friday, researchers announced the completion of a map of every neuron in the brain of a male fruit fly. The "connectome" provides a tool that can accelerate neurobiology research. But it also provides an opportunity to do some science on its own, as the connectome of a female Drosophila had been completed earlier this year . The work also provided the team behind it the opportunity to refine tools that are likely to be applied to ever-more complex nervous systems, including (potentially) those of vertebrates. The new work involved a collaboration between biologists at the Howard Hughes Medical Institute's Janelia Research Campus and computer scientists at Google—both acknowledge that neither could have done the project without the other. Preparation of an entire brain for imaging at the necessary resolution requires a distinct set of skills, as does interpreting what those images indicate. But building a complete picture of the hundreds of millions of synapses in a brain as small as the fruit fly's is a task that can't be achieved by humans in a manageable amount of time. The people behind the effort expect that in the long term, the effort will be worth it, as the connectome could give neurobiologists a valuable tool for understanding how the brain works. title: Anthropic’s $2 trillion IPO puts powerful external trustees in spotlight
raw_text: Anthropic’s prospective public-market investors must reckon with an external group of trustees that control the majority of the AI company’s board, as its planned blockbuster initial public offering forces close scrutiny of its experimental governance structure. The company’s Long-Term Benefit Trust (LTBT) is a small group of advisers created to safeguard the lab’s mission of developing AI for the long-term benefit of humanity, even as commercial pressures intensify. The trust holds no equity in Anthropic, but has significant influence, with the San Francisco-based company planning to preserve its role after a stock market debut that could value the Claude maker at as much as $2 trillion. title: Musk wins court order to block use of “Twitter,” but not “tweet” and bird logo
raw_text: On Thursday, Elon Musk’s X won a court order blocking Operation Bluebird from launching a new app taking over the Twitter name . In his opinion , Chief Judge Colm Connolly explained that Operation Bluebird was unlikely to prove that X had entirely abandoned the Twitter name. Therefore, X was likely to succeed on trademark infringement and dilution claims tied to the platform’s former name. Most compellingly, X argued that it still uses the Twitter name in the current listing for the X app in Apple’s App Store. In the first sentence of that listing, written in the same size font as the rest of the text, a single clause clinched the early court win for X by stating, “Welcome to X (formerly known as Twitter).” Read full article Comments

title: Trump White House just tossed a grenade into international space relations
raw_text: The normally genteel world of international space policy turned ugly this week as several prominent US space companies—including SpaceX, Blue Origin, Stoke Space, K2, and Starcloud—pulled out of a high-profile French space summit organized by the country's president, Emmanuel Macron. Politico first reported the diplomatic turmoil, saying that the White House "pressured" US space companies to skip Macron's space summit in Paris next week. Since then, the companies have largely pulled out of the meeting without commenting publicly, though some US representation remains on the two-day program . Multiple sources confirmed to Ars that an official with the White House Office of Science and Technology Policy, or OSTP, led the call with US space companies late last week. The call was convened in response to queries from US industry about the French meeting, which is not part of the traditional circuit of international space conferences. Read full article Comments

title: Nearly impossible? How Fairphone built the ethical, repairable Fairphone Gen 6+
raw_text: Smartphone longevity didn't used to matter. In the past, before you could wear out or break a phone, there was always some shiny new thing to buy. Today, we expect our smartphones to go the distance, but they've also become less repairable and, in many cases, more fragile. Fairphone, a Dutch smartphone maker that has just entered the US market, thinks about phones differently. The new $650 Fairphone Gen 6+ is designed both for longevity and easy repairability. There are trade-offs to this approach if you're used to the standard glass and aluminum sandwiches filled with glue, gaskets, and teeny-tiny screws. But the drawbacks could be worth it for the right buyer. Fairphone CTO Chandler Hatton told Ars that Fairphone's goal is to provide a compelling mobile experience while also enabling the user to "fully own" their device. At the end of the day, this is what a lot of people say they want in a smartphone. Take it apart, put it back together These days, Google, Samsung, and Apple support phones with software updates for the better part of a decade, but will the hardware last that long? And what happens when it needs a repair? You may be out of luck or out a lot of money, but Fairphone prioritizes the self-repair experience. Read full article Comments

title: Limiting Risk in the Face of Uncertainty
raw_text: If you save for retirement when you are young, the standard advice is to emphasize stock-based exchange-traded funds (ETFs) or mutual funds. Stocks increase and decrease in dramatic ways that no one can predict reliably, so this approach carries some risk. Fortunately for US stock market investors, that risk has historically been rewarded, on average and over the long term, with high returns. As you approach retirement and need to rely on investments to cover living expenses, the standard advice is to shift your portfolio toward bond-based ETFs or mutual funds. Bonds have had fewer and less dramatic booms and busts. For this reason, they are generally considered less risky than stocks. On average, over the long term, bonds’ safety has meant lower, more reliable returns than stocks. Risk makes less sense for ALA right now. Because of its financial deficit , the Association needs stability. Therefore, in April, ALA’s Endowment Trustees updated the target allocation for the Association’s investment portfolio, reducing our holdings of stocks from 50% to 40%, and increasing ALA’s holdings of bonds from 30% to 40%. As a result, we are sacrificing some projected returns to limit projected risk. If stocks boom as they have in the past few years, ALA’s portfolio will not increase as much as it would have. title: Prentenboeken in Papiamentu: een feest van herkenning
raw_text: Een prentenboek vertalen lijkt eenvoudig: je zet de ene taal om in de andere. Maar hoe zorg je ervoor dat een kind zich écht herkent in een verhaal? title: Bouw je eigen AI-assistent: van losse prompts naar een digitale collega
raw_text: Veel mensen gebruiken AI als vraagbaak: je start een chat, stelt een vraag, krijgt antwoord en begint de volgende keer weer met een nieuwe chat. Een AI-assistent oftewel een ‘custom agent’ werkt net anders: het is een digitale collega die je inwerkt op een specifieke taak. De grootste winst? Die ligt in het automatiseren van repeterende werkzaamheden, zodat er meer tijd overblijft voor strategie, creativiteit en contact met jouw doelgroep. In dit artikel lees je wat een AI-assistent is en hoe je er zelf een kunt inrichten om efficiënter te kunnen werken. Wat is een AI-assistent? Een AI-assistent kun je inrichten om een specifieke taak zo goed mogelijk uit te voeren. In plaats van bij iedere nieuwe chat opnieuw uit te leggen wat je wilt, geef je de assistent vooraf context, instructies en relevante documenten mee. Daardoor begrijpt het programma jouw werkwijze beter en kan het jou consistenter en beter ondersteunen. De AI voert geen autonome taken uit zoals een AI-agent, maar werkt alleen met jouw input. Waar te beginnen? Het kan ingewikkeld klinken, maar om een assistent te kunnen inrichten hoef je geen ICT- of programmeringskennis te hebben. Vrijwel alle AI-platformen bieden de mogelijkheid om een eigen assistent te bouwen. Hierbij is de start het meest belangrijk: een AI-assistent is namelijk zo slim als de informatie waarmee je hem voedt. title: Art for Everyone: How Public Libraries Expand Access
raw_text: Introducing children to viewing, creating, and enjoying art at a young age helps them appreciate it throughout their lives. Some children are exposed to various forms of art because it is part of their daily life or because they have easy access to museums and galleries in their community. But in many areas across the country, access to museums and art galleries can be cost prohibitive. That is where the public library comes in! While some museums, including the Smithsonian Institution in Washington, D.C., offer free admission, millions of people across the country do not have easy access to them. According to the 2024 Annual Survey of Museum-Goers from the American Alliance of Museums and Wilkening Consulting, museum admission costs vary widely, from a few dollars to $40–$50 per adult at some institutions. Among U.S. adults who visit museums at least occasionally, cost was the number one barrier to visiting more often. Among frequent museum-goers, younger adults were twice as likely as seniors to be concerned about admission costs. In response to those barriers, and in an effort to enrich and inspire customers of all ages, many library systems have stepped up to provide access to art in a variety of forms. title: Secrets of Effective Upskilling
raw_text: This is an excerpt from Upskilling for Library Workers: A Guide for Future-Ready Professionals by Ann Medaille (ALA Editions, 2026). With the advent of new technologies and rapid social and economic shifts, library workers’ jobs are being transformed. Compared with a decade ago, library workers now spend more time consulting on complex research tools, teaching digital literacy classes, supporting virtual learning environments, helping users troubleshoot devices, and codesigning projects with community partners. The pace at which library staffers are called upon to learn new skills is accelerating, and workers may struggle to keep up. In addition, automation and artificial intelligence (AI) are altering many aspects of work. In the long run, technological innovations have the potential to increase productivity and lead to more interesting kinds of work, but in the short term, they often cause disruptions that can be difficult for workers to navigate. To address these changes—and manage the anxieties that come along with them—workers need constant support for skill development. While corporations may embrace upskilling to stay competitive, libraries will have to support upskilling to remain relevant. Library leaders are under greater pressure to respond rapidly to changing social and economic conditions and demonstrate that their libraries make a difference in their communities. title: Hold the Phone
raw_text: Since fall 2024, each school day at Grant High School in Portland, Oregon, has started the same way: Roughly 2,100 students line up to place their phones in gray and green Yondr pouches—the kind live performers use to prevent audience members from recording—as they enter the building. From the morning bell to dismissal, phones are sealed and can be unlocked only with special magnets near the school’s exits as students leave for the day. The high school’s effort to limit phone use on campus has received support from its educators, who say classroom engagement is on the rise, and mixed reviews from students, who dislike being cut off from their devices. But there’s been one unexpected outcome of the policy: More students are spending time in the library, where they’re browsing the collection or hanging out during free periods, says teacher-librarian Paige Battle. “They’re checking out more books, and I feel like that’s been so important in their education,” Battle says. “We’re seeing studies about students, even adults, not having the reading stamina they’ve had in the past, so I’ve been encouraged by this increase.” Roughly six in 10 parents of an 11- or 12-year-old say their child owns a smartphone, according to a 2025 Pew Research Center survey . And as more schools across the country enact phone-free policies—29 states and the District of Columbia have instituted bell-to-bell phone-free policies so far—many school libraries are experiencing a surge in popularity. title: Newsmaker: Min Jin Lee
raw_text: Min Jin Lee has notched career milestones that few authors reach. Her immigration saga Pachinko was both a National Book Award finalist and a New York Times Top 10 Best Book of 2017, and it was adapted into a television series of the same name for Apple TV. Lee is also a Guggenheim fellow and the first Korean American to hold the role of New York State author laureate. Her latest title, American Hagwon (Cardinal, September), examines the influence of Korean “cram schools” among families in the Korean diaspora. American Libraries spoke with Lee ahead of her appearance at the American Library Association’s 2026 Annual Conference and Exhibition in Chicago. She discussed her new book, the library that shaped her, and her antidote to book bans. What inspired you to focus on the education system as it relates to the movements of a middle-class Korean American family in American Hagwon ? My research process involved all these interviews—I’ve done hundreds of them, probably almost 1,000 at this point—and every single time I talked to somebody, they would mention their education path. It was such an important and controversial subject. I thought, if I had to think about the most important value for Koreans, especially in the diaspora, what would I write about? Education turned out to be a beast, because people have lots of feelings about it. In the book, the Koh family loses wealth and status as they weather betrayal and financial crises. title: Mall Wonder
raw_text: After serving its community for nearly 45 years in the same building, Escondido (Calif.) Public Library closed in April 2025 for an $11.6 million renovation. It was important to us, as the city’s lone library, to preserve access during construction. So one month later, our library opened a temporary location in a very different kind of facility: the nearby North County Mall, where services and collections were spread across six storefronts, including a former Abercrombie & Fitch clothing store. Of course, moving a library takes more than a month. Our planning took more than a year and required staff to work under tight deadlines, limited budgets, and high expectations. Here’s how we did it, and what we learned from the process. Choosing a location. It’s essential to consider whether the new location will match, improve upon, or limit access. Retailers and mall operators have already studied traffic patterns, visibility, parking, and nearby amenities. Leverage that knowledge to evaluate access. In our case, the public benefited from a highway and bus stop near the mall, and adjacency to a city park. The arrangement also gave the mall a stable civic tenant and created natural cross-traffic between library patrons and shoppers. The mall was not just available space; it was a location where public access, economic development, and community visibility could overlap. title: Dismantling Disinformation
raw_text: Library workers are well aware of the effects of book bans and censorship. Propaganda and disinformation are the flipside of the same coin. Understanding the complex relationships among these interrelated processes is more critical than ever, especially as libraries explore possible solutions and responses. The following books show how disinformation can lead to censorship and how censorship can, in turn, allow disinformation to thrive. Book Bans, Disinformation, and Cultural Erasure: The Censor­ship Movement in Libraries, Schools, and Society By Paul T. Jaeger Jaeger situates the current book-banning movement within a larger social and political effort to erase marginalized communities and culture. He provides clear definitions and examples of these processes and goals, including the roles played by technological progress and economic inequity. With accessible references (like the Beatles, Dungeons & Dragons, and Holmes and Watson) and nuanced examinations of McCarthyism, the history of libraries, and the myth of neutrality, this is a recommended read for anyone interested in a more expansive understanding of current First Amendment challenges.
